senses.gloss:
ṛṣi
(‘a man of wisdom)
------------------------------------------
Derived from the verbal root ṛṣ (‘to know’), the word ṛṣi means any person who has attained expertise and proficiency in any field of knowledge. Hence, a ṛṣi need not be a person of religious, philosophical or spiritual bent of मिन्द्. In this sense, an expert in any field of knowledge, like चरक, सुश्रुत or भास्कराचार्य, can be called a ṛṣi.
However, in a more restricted sense, only a person of spiritual wisdom, who has transcended सṁसार or transmigratory existence, can be termed a ṛṣi. Being a man of perfect chastity, with tremendous self-control and deeply devoted to truth, he is also capable of blessing the good and cursing the wicked.
Ṛṣis could have been born in all castes and classes, because they attained that state by dint of their self-effort.
The general belief is that the number of ṛṣis may be around 48,000!
Sometimes, the ṛṣis are classified into several groups. For instance, the group of seven famous sages is known as सप्तर्षिस्. The सप्तर्षिस् of the present age are: विश्वामित्र, जमदग्नि, भरद्वाज, गौतम, अत्रि, वसिष्ठ and कश्यप.
Another mode of classification is: देवर्षि, ब्रह्मर्षि, राजर्षि, महर्षि, paramarṣi, śrutarṣi and काण्डर्षि.
A sage honoured even by the देवस् or gods is a देवर्षि. One who has realised ब्रह्मन् or is an expert in the वेदस् is a ब्रह्मर्षि. A rāja or a king who has attained high spiritual states is a राजर्षि. A महर्षि is one who is considered as very great. Paramarṣi is one who has realised परमात्मन् or God. A śrutarṣi is one about whom many have heard, i.e., who is famous. A sage to whom a kāṇḍa or a section of the Veda has been revealed, is a काण्डर्षि.
Apart from the सप्तर्षिस् mentioned earlier, the following are a few of the several great ṛṣis mentioned in the Hindu scriptures: नारद, कण्व, गर्ग, वाल्मीकि, व्यास, शुक, अगस्त्य, वामदेव, अष्टावक्र, भृगु, Lomaśa, दुर्वासस्, धौम्य, सनक, मार्कण्डेय and Maudgalya.

Ṛṣipañcamī-vrata
------------------------------------------
The ऋषिपञ्चमी-व्रत is dedicated to honouring the सप्तर्षिस् or the seven sages who are highly revered figures in our tradition. They are कश्यप, अत्रि, Bhara-dvāja, विश्वामित्र, गोतम, जमदग्नि and वसिष्ठ. (According to another tradi-tion, they are: मरीचि, अत्रि, अङ्गिरस्, पुलस्त्य, Pulaha, Kratu and वसिष्ठ.) They have laid us under a deep debt by revealing spiritual knowledge and wisdom through the Vedic mantras.
The vrata can be performed by men of all the varṇas (for all practical purposes, castes). Worship can be offered to the images of the sages. Subsisting on vegetables and observing celibacy are very important in this vrata. Freedom from sins and troubles and increase of good fortune are the promised results. Women observing this vrata are promised good bodily form, beauty, happiness and pro-geny. It may be observed for seven years (i.e. seven Ṛṣipañcamīs consecutively). The seven images along with the seven kalaśas should be donated to seven ब्राह्मणस्.
Though meant for all, it has somehow become a vrata observed mostly by women.

ṛṣikā
(‘a woman ṛṣi or sage’)
------------------------------------------
The word ṛṣi means a person of intuitive knowledge and wisdom, especially a seer of Vedic hymn. Contrary to the general notion, a ṛṣi need not be a man only. There are as many as 27 ṛṣis mentioned in the Ṛgveda itself who were women (vide Bṛhaddevatā 2.82-84).
These 27 ṛṣis, called ṛṣikās, have been classified into three groups of nine persons each.
The ṛṣikās of the first group are: घोषा, Godhā, Viśvavārā, Apālā, Upaniṣat, Niṣat, Brahmajāyā-juhā, Agastyasvasā and अदिति.
The following are the ṛṣikās of the second group: इन्द्राणी, Indramātā, सरमा, Romaśā, Urvaśī, लोपामुद्रा, Nadyaḥ (= river deities), Yamī and Śāśvatī.
The third group comprises the following nine who have been specially designated as Brahmavādinīs: Śrīḥ, Lākṣā, Sārparājñī, Vāk, श्रद्धा, Medhā, दक्षिणा, Rātrī, and Sūryāsāvitrī.
The ṛṣikās of the first group have just sung hymns of praise of the gods. The second group ṛṣikās have conversed with prominent ṛṣis (sages) and gods. The ṛṣikās of the third group have identified themselves with the deities and hence have praised themselves through the hymns. Thus they are not only the ṛṣis but also the देवतास् (deities to whom the prayer is addressed.
